sections.section_title: The Household Framework -- How Timothy Should Address Each Group
sections.summary: Timothy is instructed to treat the community as family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters in all purity.

The community must honor genuinely destitute widows; widows with family should be cared for by their children or grandchildren; the self-indulgent widow is 'dead even while she lives'; and anyone who fails to provide for family 'has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.'
sections.relevance: Two statements in this section directly bear on the question. First, verse 6 declares that the self-indulgent widow 'living, has died' (zosa tethneken) -- she is spiritually dead while physically alive, her self-indulgence constituting a departure from the life that comes through hope in God. Second, verse 8 states that anyone who does not provide for relatives 'has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' The neutral reading identifies this denial as practical rather than verbal: the person may still profess faith with their mouth, but their conduct constitutes a denial of everything the faith teaches. The verb arneisthai ('to deny') is the same word used for Peter's denial of Jesus and in 2 Timothy 2:12 ('if we deny him, he will deny us'). The passage treats behavior as capable of constituting denial of the faith -- not merely a lapse within a secure standing, but a genuine denial that renders the person worse than those who never believed.
key_phrases: she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives
he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever

sections.summary: Enrolled widows must be at least sixty years old, have been the wife of one husband, and have a demonstrated reputation for good works including raising children, showing hospitality, washing the saints' feet, caring for the afflicted, and pursuing every kind of good.

sections.section_title: Younger Widows -- The Problem and the Solution
sections.summary: Younger widows should not be enrolled because their desires draw them away from Christ, leading them to break their pledge and incur condemnation; they become idle, gossiping, and meddling; Paul recommends they marry, bear children, and manage households -- because some have already strayed after Satan.
sections.relevance: Verse 15 states that 'some have already strayed after Satan' (ede gar tines exetrapesan opiso tou Satana). The neutral reading emphasizes that this is not a theoretical warning but a report of events that have already occurred. The verb ektrepesthai ('to turn aside, to stray') is the same word used in 1:6 for those who swerved from sound teaching. The adverb ede ('already') confirms these are accomplished departures. The passage is part of the letter's consistent pattern: some have swerved (1:6), some have shipwrecked their faith (1:19), some will depart from the faith (4:1), and now some have already strayed after Satan (5:15). Additionally, verse 12 describes younger widows incurring condemnation (krima) for abandoning their pledge. The passage treats departure from the community of faith as a real and present reality, not a theoretical impossibility.
key_phrases: when their passions draw them away from Christ
incur condemnation for having abandoned their first pledge
some have already strayed after Satan

sections.summary: Believing women with widowed relatives must care for them so the church is not burdened and can devote its resources to the truly destitute widows.

sections.section_title: Elders Who Rule Well -- Double Honor
sections.summary: Elders who govern well deserve double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching, grounded in Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus (Luke 10:7), both cited as Scripture.

sections.section_title: Accusations Against Elders -- Due Process and Impartiality
sections.summary: Accusations against elders require two or three witnesses per the Torah's standard; confirmed sinners receive public rebuke for deterrence; Timothy is solemnly charged before God, Christ Jesus, and the elect angels to act without prejudgment or partiality.

sections.section_title: Timothy's Personal Conduct -- Purity, Health, and the Visibility of Character
sections.summary: Timothy must not rush ordination or share in others' sins, must keep himself pure, may use a little wine for health (correcting ascetic distortion), and can trust that character -- both sins and good works -- will eventually reveal itself.
